SELECTION_NARRATIVE: This watershed is characterized by a shallow water table with groundwater dependent ecosystems present throughout.  Small wetlands and groundwater fed springs, seeps, fens and wet meadow ecosystems are common and serve as recharge areas for the Sheyenne Delta Aquifer, which underlies the entire watershed. SELECTION_NARRATIVE: Watershed is a stronghold for native fish habitat and populations.  Reducing road densities would improve water quality by reducing sediment inputs to streams and would reduce risk of future road or culver failures that could further impair the ecosystem.  NEPA covering watershed improvement work is complete (includes over 50 miles of road decommissioning and/or storage) which was done in conjunction with the Fallen Bear Project, incorporating timber, engineering, wildlife and fuels activities.  Planned watershed improvement work aligns with national and regional strategies and forest plan. Watershed is within the same 5th code HUC as future District priority watersheds (e.g. Gold Creek). High runoff and or flooding may cause road/culvert or bridge failure. Implementation of road work would create jobs for contractors. Watershed improvement work would be cost effective if done in conjunction with current timber sale contract work within the area.  On-the-ground accomplishments would be realized in FY12 and FY13.  The Bruin Creek watershed currently has a WCATT watershed condition rating of “FAR”.  By reducing road densities within the HUC the watershed condition rating would move closer to a “FP” condition.  If road densities are not reduced there would be a risk of the watershed condition moving to an “IF” condition if road failures were to occur increasing stream sedimentation and negatively impacting fish habitat.  Watershed is also located within the St. Joe Wild and Scenic River corridor.
WRAP_NAME: Bruin Creek 2011 Watershed Action Plan

SELECTION_NARRATIVE: The Lower South Fork Two Medicine River is a unique watershed located just south of Glacier National Park and west of the Black Feet Indian Reservation. The Rocky Mountain Travel Plan has been completed and the implementation of road decommissioning is a high forest priority. The L&C plans to continue the road work which will have the benefit of lowering the road densities which will eliminate chronic sediment supplies to streams, slowing the spread of noxious weeds and improve the overall watersheds hydrologic function. Grazing within the watershed has resulted in soil damage, streambank/riparian corridor degradation, degraded westslope cutthroat trout habitat, and the spread of invasive weeds. Native species i.e. cutthroat trout are threatened by rainbow trout hybridization and brook trout competition. Potential partnerships will include the Blackfeet Tribe, Glacier Conservation District, Montana Fish Wildlife and Parks, and Trout Unlimited.

SELECTION_NARRATIVE: In general the Shields River watershed is a productive area for range, wildlife, and timber.  The Shields River, its tributaries, and headwaters form an extensive stream system offering historic habitat for native Yellowstone Cutthroat Trout (YCT).   Nonnative brook trout present a dire threat to the persistence of YCT in the upper Shields River basin.  Extensive survey and study of movements of fishes by the Wildlife Conservation Society and agency partners indicate brook trout are undergoing a current and rapid invasion in the upper Shields River watershed, resulting in displacement of YCT. Without intervention, this population would likely be lost within a few decades. Although the brook trout invasion is troubling, extensive analyses of tissue samples have found no evidence of rainbow trout hybridization in the YCT within the any of the streams sampled.  As nonhybridized fish, these YCT populations have tremendous conservation value and are of the highest conservation priority.
WRAP_NAME: WATERSHED RESTORATION ACTION PLAN - Custer Gallatin National Forest: Shields River - Bennett Creek

SELECTION_NARRATIVE: The Headwater of Sheep Creek is a State 303d listed stream for metals, mercury, and pathogens. Legacy road decommissioning is a high priority for the Lewis and Clark National Forest. The Little Belts Travel Plan has been completed and implementation of road decommissioning has commenced within the watershed.  The watershed was extensively logged resulting in high road densities which contribute chronic sediment to streams and disrupts the natural hydrologic function across the watershed. The L&C plans to continue road decommissioning work which will have the benefits of lowering the road density within the watershed, reducing the chronic sediment inputs to streams and improve hydrologic function of the drainage.  Another high sediment source is from winter traction sanding along State Highway 89 resulting in improper stream function and has degraded westslope cutthroat trout habitat. SELECTION_NARRATIVE: The Bertie Lord watershed is located within the Martin Creek project area on the Sula Ranger District. The Martin Creek project involves decommissioning of non-system, historical roads that are not needed for future management. The project analyzed a total of 122 miles of historic roads and identified 63 miles to be decommissioned and 59 miles to be included as part of the transportation system and stored for future use. Only 20 miles out the 63 miles of decommissioning will require active treatment, the remainder were previously treated or have naturally recovered. The Bertie Lord watershed contains 8 miles of roads that will require active decommissioning treatment.  The project will protect and improve watershed, soils, and fisheries resources and also meet the intent of the Water Quality Restoration Plan and TMDL requirements for the East Fork Bitterroot River.  We currently have a partnership agreement with Trout Unlimited to complete restoration work in this priority watershed and the overall Martin Creek project area.
WRAP_NAME: Bertie Lord Watershed Restoration Action Plan

SELECTION_NARRATIVE: The Upper Sleeping Child watershed is located within the  Darby Lumber Lands project area and is one the highest priorities for watershed rehabilitation on the forest. Upper Sleeping Child contains several sections of former private “checkerboard” sections that were recently acquired by the USFS. Management by former landowner included liquidation of the timber base with little resource consideration.  Sub-standard and poorly located roads built by the former land owner are in poor condition and are not needed for future timber management.  High severity fire activity in 2000 added to watershed sensitivity, precipitation effectiveness, and increased soil loss.  Road densities, watershed condition, and stream channel condition all fall short of Forest Plan desired conditions.  Bull Trout (Sleeping Child watershed), West Slope cutthroat (Rye Creek watershed), INFISH compliance and State Impaired Waters (303(d) listed) compliance would benefit/improve from road decomissioning and storage activities. Phase 1 of the Darby Lumber Lands project would include decommissioning of former landowner roads and historic FS roads in the Upper Sleeping Child and Rye Creek watersheds.  Total miles to be decomissioned are approximately 60 miles, split between 3 years of implementation (FY13 through FY15).   We are currently pursing additional partner funding for project implementation but is not guaranteed at this time.
WRAP_NAME: Upper Sleeping Child Watershed Restoration Action Plan
